transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you, too. Well, it's a bit of a long story, I suppose, but the main thing that made me come in is that my eating has just gotten all turned around lately. Completely topsy-turvy. 

You know, when you get to be my age and you're just keeping house for yourself, it's sometimes hard to find the motivation to make a big meal, but this is different. It's like... well, some days I'll be sitting in my chair, maybe watching a program or just looking out the front window, and I'll look up at the clock and realize it's nearly four in the afternoon and I've completely forgotten to eat lunch. It just slips my mind entirely, like I don't even have a stomach. 

But then, on other days, I just don't know what comes over me. I'll find myself just standing right there at the kitchen counter—not even sitting down at the table with a proper plate like a civilized person—and I'll just be eating crackers, or whatever sweets I have tucked away in the cupboard. Just one after the other. And the strangest part of it all is that nothing even tastes right. It all just tastes like cardboard or dust, but I just stand there and keep eating it anyway. I was telling my neighbor about it the other day, and she said I really ought to come talk to someone, because I used to be such a routine person—breakfast at eight, lunch at noon sharp—and now I just don't know what's happening with my appetite at all. It's just very upsetting to not even enjoy a simple cookie anymore, you know?
Aside from your appetite, have you noticed any other changes lately, such as difficulty keeping track of your appointments or forgetting where you've put things around the house?

Well, no, not really. I mean, my memory has always been sharp as a tack, thank heavens. I've always been the sort of person who remembers everybody's birthday—nieces, nephews, even the neighbor's children. I still send out cards, you know, the nice ones you get at the pharmacy, not those cheap ones from the dollar store. And as for my appointments, I have this lovely little floral calendar right by the telephone in the hallway. I write everything down the minute I schedule it. Hairdresser on Tuesdays, church circle on Thursdays... I haven't missed a single one. 

And my house, well, everything has its place. My mother always said, "A place for everything and everything in its place," and I've lived by that my whole life. My keys go in the little ceramic bowl by the door—the one my grandson made for me in third grade, it's painted a lovely shade of blue, though the glaze is chipping just a bit on the rim. My reading glasses are always on the side table next to my armchair, right by my crossword puzzle books. So no, I haven't been misplacing things or forgetting where I put them. I might walk into a room and wonder what I went in there for, but that's just normal for someone my age, isn't it? You just retrace your steps and it comes right back to you. But nothing like losing my keys or forgetting appointments, no, nothing like that at all. My mind is still perfectly clear on those things, it's just this business with the eating that has me so out of sorts.
Beyond the changes in your appetite, have you been feeling a persistent sense of sadness or a loss of interest in the hobbies and activities you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose I have been. It's... it's hard to explain, really, because I've always been such a cheerful person. My husband, God rest his soul, used to call me his little ray of sunshine. But lately, it's just... well, most mornings I wake up with this terribly heavy, low feeling. It's right here in my chest, just pressing down on me. It feels like the color has completely gone out of the day before I even manage to get out of bed and get dressed. 

I used to love my mornings, you know. I'd get up, put the kettle on, and listen to the birds outside the kitchen window. I have a little feeder out there, the red plastic kind that the cardinals just love. I used to make a whole ritual of it, watching them bicker over the sunflower seeds while I drank my tea. But now, I just lie there under the covers, and the room feels so gray. Even when the sun is shining right through the lace curtains—the ones I bought at that lovely little boutique downtown before it closed—it just feels dreary. 

And you asked about my hobbies... well, I used to be quite the knitter. I've knitted blankets for every single baby born in our church congregation for the last fifteen years. Soft pastel yarns, always with a little scalloped edge. I had a whole basket of yarn sitting right next to my armchair, just waiting for the next project. But the last few months, I just look at the needles and I can't bring myself to pick them up. The thought of counting stitches just feels exhausting, like climbing a mountain. I tried to start a little yellow cardigan for my neighbor's new grandbaby a few weeks ago, but I only got through the ribbing before I just... put it back in the basket. It's still sitting there, gathering dust. I just don't have the heart for it anymore. It's like all the joy has just been drained right out of the things that used to make me so happy, and I'm just left with this awful, heavy sadness that follows me around the house all day long.
Have you ever felt this way before, perhaps years ago, or is this the first time you have experienced such a deep, persistent sadness?

Well, no, I've never felt quite like this before. That's the strange thing about it, isn't it? I mean, of course, I've had sad days. When Arthur passed—that's my husband, Arthur—oh, I was devastated, naturally. Anyone would be. We were married for forty-seven years, you know. We met at a church social when I was just nineteen, and he was wearing this awful plaid tie, but he had the kindest eyes. Anyway, when he died, I cried for months. But that was a different kind of sadness. That was grief, and it made sense. I knew why I was crying. I'd look at his empty armchair and I'd weep, but eventually, the pain softened, the way people tell you it will. I started going back to my church circle, I started knitting again, I even took a little bus tour up to Nova Scotia with my sister-in-law, Betty, about five years ago. 

But this... this is entirely different. There's no reason for it. Nobody died, nothing terrible happened. It just sort of crept up on me. I've been trying to pinpoint exactly when it started, because I like to be precise about these things, and I'd say this low, colorless stretch has been with me for about a year and two months now. Yes, it was right around the end of October, the year before last, because I remember I didn't even put out my ceramic pumpkins on the front porch for Halloween. I usually always put them out—I have three of them, a big one, a medium one, and a little tiny one that lights up inside. The neighborhood children always loved them. But that year, I just looked at the box in the hall closet and I couldn't muster the energy to carry it out to the porch. And it's just been like that ever since. A whole year and two months of waking up feeling like I'm made of lead, and nothing seems to shake it. I've tried drinking chamomile tea, I've tried listening to the upbeat music on the radio, but nothing works. It's just a constant, heavy blanket over everything, and it's the first time in my seventy-four years I've ever experienced anything quite so stubborn and awful.
Are there days when this heavy feeling in your chest is so overwhelming that you find yourself unable to get out of bed or perform your essential daily tasks, like bathing or dressing yourself?

Well, I do force myself up eventually. I mean, I still manage to stay in my own home, thank heavens, and I make sure I'm washed and dressed, even if it's just putting on my comfortable housecoat—the pink chenille one, it has these lovely big pockets, you know, and it's so warm. I wouldn't let myself completely go to seed. But... well, I know I was going on earlier about my floral calendar and how I never miss a thing, but if I'm being completely honest with you... and I suppose I have to be... this heavy feeling *has* been making me slip up. It's not my memory failing, it's just... I can't seem to muster the will. 

Like my craft classes, for instance. I used to teach a little class at the community center on Wednesday afternoons. We did all sorts of lovely projects—making seasonal wreaths, painting wooden birdhouses, decorating mason jars for the holidays. The ladies always looked forward to it, especially Mrs. Higgins, who doesn't get out much since her hip replacement. But I just... I stopped teaching them. I called the director a few months ago and told them I needed a break, and I haven't been back. The thought of standing up there and trying to be cheerful and instruct people... it was just too much to bear.

And the other things... I find myself putting off things that used to be completely routine. I'll look at the telephone, knowing I'm supposed to return a call from my niece—she just had a baby, little Thomas, such a sweet boy—but I just let it ring. I've missed calls, I've skipped family tasks I used to handle so carefully, like organizing the Sunday dinners or sending out the church bulletin updates. I've even missed a few appointments, which I know I said I didn't do! But I didn't *forget* them, you see, I just looked at the calendar and thought, "I can't possibly face the hairdresser today," and I just let it pass. Now, I find I have to rely more on little reminder notes just to get the bare minimum done, sticking them on the refrigerator with my strawberry magnets, and even then, I just put off the things that used to be second nature. It's just so unlike me, doctor, to let these things slide.

You mentioned this is the first time you have felt this specific way in your seventy-four years, but have you ever experienced any other periods in your life—perhaps years before this current stretch began—where you felt this same heavy, persistent sadness and loss of interest for several weeks or more?

Well, no, absolutely not. I really meant it when I said this is the very first time. I've never had anything like this happen before, not even for a few weeks. I was always the one keeping everyone else's spirits up, you see. 

Even during the really hard times... like back in nineteen eighty-two, when Arthur lost his job at the manufacturing plant. They closed the whole place down right before Thanksgiving, laid off half the men in town. It was just dreadful. A lot of the wives were just beside themselves, crying in the aisles at the grocery store, not knowing how they were going to afford Christmas presents for the children or keep the heat on. But I didn't fall apart. I didn't get heavy or lose my interest in things. I just rolled up my sleeves. I started baking pies—apple, cherry, and a lovely strawberry-rhubarb using my grandmother's recipe—and I sold them to the local diner to help make ends meet until Arthur got hired on at the hardware store. I never once stayed in bed. 

If I ever felt even a little bit blue back then, or really at any point in my life, I'd just find something productive to do. I'd scrub the baseboards or polish the silver. We have this beautiful silver tea service that Arthur's mother gave us for our wedding, and it has all these intricate little floral engravings on the handles that take just hours to clean properly with a soft cloth and the polish. It's tedious work, but by the time I was finished with something like that, I'd feel right as rain again. 

So, no, I keep searching my memory, thinking maybe when the boys went off to college—I have two boys, David and Michael, David is an accountant and Michael teaches middle school—maybe I felt it then? People always talk about empty nest syndrome and how it ruins a mother. But no, I was sad they were leaving, of course, but I still went to my garden club every Tuesday. I still grew my prize-winning blue hydrangeas, the big mophead ones that need the soil to be just the right acidity. I never stopped living my life, I never stopped wanting to do my hobbies. This terrible, gray blanket feeling is completely new to me, which is why it's so very frustrating to deal with now.

inference.note: The patient explicitly states this is the first episode of this nature in her life and denies any previous episodes of depression, which rules out Recurrent Depressive Disorder (F33). Given the duration of over a year and the severity of symptoms, F32.2 (Major depressive disorder, single episode, severe without psychotic symptoms) is the most appropriate candidate.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent, pervasive low mood, anhedonia, and fatigue lasting over 14 months, which significantly impairs her social and occupational functioning. While she denies a history of mania, the duration (exceeding 1 year) and the recurrence of symptoms (though she describes this as a single long episode, the clinical presentation fits a major depressive episode) lead to a diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder, currently moderate.
